messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Karan Mehta was thirty when the mortar strike caught him in the market square. He had been standing with a coil of heavy twine in his hands, watching dust rise in thick, ochre clouds, when a sharp, sudden explosion tore through the air. The concussive blast drove the breath from his lungs. He felt his knees buckle and his body drop into a low, braced crouch, shoulders hunched, arms wrapped tight against his ribs. In that moment, the thick wool of his vest felt impossibly heavy, and the acrid stench of cordite and sun-baked earth filled his nose. What frightened him most was the sheer loss of control, the way the chaos unfolded around him while he remained locked in place, the twine slipping from his fingers. His wife, sitting beside him in the living room years later, would often watch him sit at his own kitchen table and suddenly feel his body return to that exact crouched position, spine stiff, bracing against a blow that had already passed. When Karan returned home, his posture never fully uncoiled. He had come to believe that what had happened in the square was so extreme it seemed to belong to someone else; the story of the blast and the dust felt almost unreal, hard to believe it actually happened to him. His world had shifted. He began to see the environment as a place of latent threat, where danger could materialize without invitation. Nothing in his daily routine felt meaningful anymore, and he questioned whether the steady, deliberate craft that had once defined him was still within his reach. He no longer felt capable of doing the things that had once structured his days, and a quiet resignation settled over his home. Over the weeks and months, Karan found himself constantly on guard. His muscles stayed coiled, his breathing shallow, his eyes tracking the periphery of every room. Ordinary sounds—a car door slamming, a paint can lid popping off, a neighbor’s hammer—would make him jump, his body snapping into that same braced position before his mind had time to catch up. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger. He worked hard at keeping busy with other things. He spent long hours in his sunlit studio, mixing pigments, priming canvases, and organizing his brushes. The sharp, chemical tang of turpentine and gesso sometimes triggered the old ochre-dust scent, pulling his attention back to the market square. He avoided the evening news, turning away from broadcasts about distant conflicts and urban emergencies, certain that another report about a blast would unravel his composure. He went over and over why the event had fallen to him, why he had been left there standing while others moved on, his thoughts circling the same questions like a wheel on a track. Now at fifty-three, Karan has begun to notice how his capabilities feel distant even within his own studio. A dropped brush or a sudden gust of wind rattling the windows makes him pause, his startle reflex quick, his body on alert. The loss of meaning lingers in his quiet evenings and his solitary meals, even as he continues to paint. His PCL-5 score of 34 maps closely to the steady accumulation of these days. What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon when a passing garbage truck’s hydraulic lift threw a loud bang against the pavement. He had dropped his palette knife, his shoulders rising instinctively, and the grief on recall surged up so completely that he sat on the studio floor, waiting for the wave to pass. He is hoping to find a way to let his body unclench, to trust that the world is not always on the verge of collapsing, and to rediscover the steady purpose that once guided his hands.
